Issued at 1239 PM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: Temperatures are soaring into the 60s this afternoon 
as a surface trough races eastward.  This trough continues to also 
drop dew points significantly, leading to near or critical RH values 
over south central South Dakota. Satellite early this afternoon 
shows a confined area of mid-lvl clouds associated with strong 
dPVA pivoting northeast through the Dakotas this afternoon. It's
a non- zero chance that an isolated sprinkle to high based 
shower could pass through areas from Gregory to Mitchell to 
Huron and Brookings into early evening. Elsewhere the biggest 
impacts will be from a turning wind direction behind the passing
surface trough into the evening. 

TONIGHT: Skies will clear throughout the region as the upper 
wave moves into eastern North Dakota and northern Minnesota. A 
west southwest wind may relax slightly by daybreak with any 
meaningful clouds north of the area. The mixy winds are expected
to keep overnight low temperatures in the upper 30s to lower 
40s. It should be noted that record warm low temperatures are 
likely to be set at all the climate stations by midnight. 

THURSDAY: A surface ridge sliding through the Plains will keep winds 
light and skies sunny.  Temperatures continue to stay above normal, 
with highs in the 50s in most locations and 60s south of Highway 20. 
 Recent trends have suggested that even with light winds, recent dry 
conditions may let temperatures warm above the NBM deterministic.

FRIDAY: The passage of the 850mb ridge axis early Thursday evening 
will usher in stronger low-lvl warm advection and return flow into 
the Plains ahead of another very deep trough that develops west of 
the Rockies.  The orientation and depth of this trough will have a 
better opportunity pulling in some Gulf moisture with a higher mid-
lvl Pacific moisture stream moving northeast as well. By Friday 
morning a surface warm front will advance through the area along 
with considerable stratus and seasonally significant dew points
near 50 degrees. The orientation of the surface and low-lvl 
flow would favor strong wind gusts through the day and into the 
evening with soundings indicating potential to tap into the 45+ 
knots of flow within the 850mb layer. NBM probabilities for 
reaching 45 mph (advisory criteria) are near 70% for the 
afternoon, and have blended in some 90th percentile data to 
account for potential. Temperatures will be a bit more uncertain
given the stratus layer. 25/75th percentile data suggests the 
range of high temperatures may end up in the upper 50s to lower 
60s. If stratus clears the 90th percentile temperatures are in 
the middle 60s. 

SATURDAY:  Pieces of the upper trough begin to break apart and move 
into the Northern Plains Friday evening. A surface front slides 
through the night, bringing at least low risks for a few showers 
within a narrow channel of warm advection ahead of the boundary. The 
latest guidance continues to suggest that this broad upper 
trough splits into two distinct waves as it moves east this 
weekend, though uncertainty on where these features track is 
still a bit uncertain. Most guidance continues to support 
pushing the surface front into eastern Nebraska and northwest 
Iowa during the day, with the potential for redevelopment of 
rain as stronger frontogenesis develops Saturday afternoon and 
evening. Generally over the course of the last 2-3 days 
model/ensemble guidance continues to support increased rain 
risks, but the favored locations have been slipping further 
southeast into Iowa/Nebraska/southern Minnesota.

SUNDAY-TUESDAY:  Cool Canadian high pressure dips into the Plains as 
the holiday week begins, dropping temperatures near to slightly 
below normals. A relative flat/zonal flow will prevent any major 
impactful systems, but could produce minor systems ahead of the 
holiday.  The deterministic model "now you see it, now you don't" 
may continue on a run to run bases given the pattern.  From an 
ensemble perspective there are enough signals from multiple 
runs to hit at precipitation, but low probabilities of 
measurable QPF Tuesday reside anywhere from 30-60% (higher 
towards western SD/NE) and probabilities for anything over 0.10"
remain considerable lower and spread over large areas. All this
to say, no major systems ahead, but at least some potential
systems for travelers to monitor.
